strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: replacing a single fixed LoRA with a learnable basis of LoRAs plus a lightweight CLIP-based router for visual analogy completion is a natural and novel application of the weight-basis insight (Dravid et al.) to a task setting where test-time per-task LoRA optimization is infeasible.

The proposed design is sensible and well-reasoned: full analogy triplet is fed via extended attention to Flux.1-Kontext for detail preservation, while CLIP encodings are reserved for LoRA selection; joint training of basis and router avoids the cost of Dravid et al.'s 65k independently trained LoRAs.

Reasonably thorough evaluation: comparisons against four baselines including a capacity-matched single-LoRA control, both automated metrics and a 2AFC user study (33 users, 45 pairs), a validation of the Gemma-3 VLM judge against human preferences (66.7% user-VLM agreement vs 74.2% user-user agreement), and ablations over basis size N, rank r, activation choice, encoder input layout, and encoder backbone (SigLIP2).

Useful analysis beyond headline numbers: Fig. 7 demonstrates the model is genuinely driven by the reference pair (fine-grained details like crystal count/color), distinguishing analogy-based editing from prompt-only editing — a check many baselines fail.

Custom evaluation set construction is documented in detail (prompts, LoRA sources, filtering), aiding reproducibility, and the paper discusses limitations of generalization to tasks far from the training corpus.
weaknesses: The evaluation benchmark is self-constructed and filtered in ways that could favor the proposed method: in-domain prompts are filtered by 'Flux.1-Kontext fails to produce a meaningful edit' removal, and out-of-domain analogies come from community Flux-Kontext LoRAs. The authors' own single-LoRA baseline is trained by them on the same data, which is fair, but there is no independent, third-party benchmark to corroborate the generalization claims.

The improvement over the simplest, capacity-matched baseline (single LoRA r=128) is modest: 57.9% pairwise VLM win rate (57.6% in Fig. 6), and LoRWeB actually has slightly lower preservation and LPIPS/CLIP-dir scores than this baseline (Tab. 1 / Tab. S2). The case that a basis is necessary, rather than the stronger training recipe, would benefit from deeper analysis (e.g., visualization of learned routing coefficients, interpretability of basis elements, or comparisons on a public held-out suite).

Several conclusions rest on a single VLM judge (Gemma-3); while human alignment is reported, the small user study (33 users, 45 pairs) and the modest win margins make some comparisons (especially vs. LoRA r=128 and RelationAdapter) statistically fragile despite Wilson intervals.

No analysis of why the learned basis generalizes, no exploration of negative/signed combinations beyond a brief Tanh note, and the 'space of LoRAs' framing is more conceptual than substantiated; the paper does not verify that basis elements specialize to distinct transformation types.

Writing has noticeable typos and inconsistencies ('Our appraoch', 'Relation Aadpter', figure axis label 'Aadpter', Fig. S1 typo-heavy caption), and results are presented mostly as figures/plots whose exact values only appear in a supplementary table.
The paper would be strengthened by releasing quantitative results on the official Relation252k unseen split separately from the custom set, and by a societal-impact discussion, which is absent.

strengths: The core idea—replacing a single adaptation module with a learned basis of LoRAs dynamically mixed by a lightweight router for visual analogy completion—is sensible and clearly motivated, connecting recent weight-space findings [12] with in-context analogy editing.

The evaluation is relatively thorough for this line of work: automated metrics (LPIPS, CLIP directional), a VLM-based scoring protocol with its prompts released, a 2AFC user study (33 users), and an analysis of the VLM metric's alignment with human agreement (66.7% user–VLM vs 74.2% user–user).

The paper includes meaningful ablations on basis size, rank, normalization function, encoder choice, and encoder input layout, plus an explicit experiment (Fig. 7) showing the model genuinely uses the analogy pair rather than just the prompt—a concern worth addressing.
Limitations are honestly acknowledged, and implementation details (hyperparameters, checkpoints, community LoRA sources) are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method is essentially a standard mixture-of-LoRAs/router (cf. MoLE, MoE-LoRA, LoraHub [64]) applied on top of an existing in-context editing setup (RelationAdapter-style composite 2×2 conditioning on Flux.1-Kontext). The 'space of LoRAs' framing is directly borrowed from Dravid et al. [12], and the router is a single softmax over learned keys (Eq. 4). Each component is well-trodden; the contribution is their combination in a new task, which reads as incremental.

The margin over the most important control—the single LoRA of matched capacity—is small and possibly within noise. Pairwise win rates vs the r=128 LoRA are only 57.6% (user) and 57.9% (VLM), with overlapping Wilson intervals in Fig. 6. In Table 1, several ablated variants (N=16, +2×2 Enc. Input) actually match or beat the full model on several metrics, and no statistical significance is reported for the main comparisons.

The evaluation set is self-constructed and partially circular. The 540-triplet set is built by the authors; 'in-domain' unseen analogies are generated by Flux.1-Kontext itself, and 'out-of-domain' analogies come from 18 Flux community style LoRAs—precisely the kind of specialization a linear LoRA mixture is structurally suited to represent. There is no evaluation on a standard, independently curated benchmark, which weakens the SOTA claim.

The prompts supplied alongside the analogy pair risk leaking the task identity into both the model and the VLM judge; Fig. 7 shows the model relies on the pair, but the extent to which the baseline's poor performance stems from prompt ambiguity vs the proposed architecture is not disentangled (e.g., a baseline without prompts is not reported).

The paper is noticeably sloppy: repeated typos ('Aadpter' in Figures 4, S2 and Table captions, 'LoRBA', 'analoy', 'varity', 'appraoch', 'Gemna-3', 'low-rank adaption', 'cloths'), rendering errors (R_{768}), and inconsistent experiment labels in Table 1 ('+ r = 16' changes N implicitly). For a camera-ready-quality venue, this lack of polish undermines confidence in overall care.

Several claims are under-supported: the Tanh underperformance explanation is speculative; the 'significantly improves generalization to unseen visual transformations' claim rests mostly on the authors' own dataset; and the strongest baseline comparisons (VisualCloze, EditTransfer) appear from Table S2 to be notably weaker models, making headline wins less informative.

Potential failure modes of the router—e.g., collapsing to a few basis LoRAs, sensitivity to N, behavior at higher resolution than 512×512 training resolution—are not analyzed, and no visualization of the learned coefficients or basis specialization is provided, despite the interpretability framing.

strengths: The core idea—replacing a single task-adaptation LoRA with a jointly learned basis of LoRA modules that are dynamically mixed at inference time via a lightweight encoder—is elegant, well-motivated by prior observations about LoRA weight spaces [12], and clearly positioned against both single-LoRA fine-tuning and infeasible test-time per-task LoRA training/hypernetworks.

The method is technically simple yet effective, and the design choices (CLIP encodings used only for routing while the full triplet goes through extended attention for detail preservation) are sensible and well justified.

Evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: four baselines (including a capacity-matched single-LoRA control, which is the most important comparison), multiple complementary metrics (LPIPS, CLIP directional, VLM-based absolute scores, 2AFC pairwise VLM, and a 33-user human study), and the VLM metric is validated against human agreement (66.7% user–VLM vs. 74.2% user–user agreement), which many papers omit.

The ablation study is genuinely useful: it isolates basis size vs. rank, tests alternative normalization (Tanh), encoder backbones (SigLIP2), encoder input layouts, and shows that naive capacity increases do not help—supporting the paper's central hypothesis about basis compositionality rather than raw capacity.

The experiment in Fig. 7 (same prompt, different reference pairs) directly demonstrates the model performs analogy-driven editing rather than prompt-driven editing, addressing a key confound in this task.
The paper is clearly written, the method is easy to follow, and code/data release is promised, aiding reproducibility; the custom benchmark construction and prompt lists are documented in detail.
weaknesses: The strongest claim (state-of-the-art, significant generalization gains) rests on a small margin over the capacity-matched single-LoRA baseline: the head-to-head win rates are only ~57.6/42.4 (user) and ~57.9/42.1 (VLM), and no statistical significance tests (e.g., binomial tests or bootstrap CIs) are reported. Gains over weaker baselines (Edit Transfer, VisualCloze) are large but those are less competitive; against the proper control the improvement is modest.

The evaluation benchmark is self-constructed and small (540 triplets, 90–100 tasks), and its construction has a potential circularity concern: in-domain analogy pairs are generated and filtered by Flux.1-Kontext succeeding on the edit, i.e., the same backbone family LoRWeB is built on. Since three baselines (RelationAdapter, VisualCloze, Edit Transfer) are built on Flux.1-Dev, part of LoRWeB's advantage may stem from the stronger underlying editing model rather than the LoRA-basis mechanism. The capacity-matched Kontext LoRA is the only clean control, and there the margin is thin.

Ablation anomalies are not fully explained: e.g., r=16 alone (Table 1) drops drastically in Edit Accuracy (4.92) and Pairwise VLM against RA (49.6, below 50%), and the Tanh variant collapses almost uniformly; the paper offers only brief hypotheses. More analysis of when/why the basis mechanism fails (e.g., coefficient distributions, which LoRAs are selected per task) would strengthen the scientific case that the basis is actually being used compositionally rather than as a large single adapter.

The 'unseen transformation' evaluation includes 18 community LoRAs (many style-transfer tasks, e.g., Ghibli, clay toy, pop art) that resemble training-task categories in Relation252k; the degree to which the test set truly covers out-of-distribution transformations could be argued further.

Some claims of novelty should be tempered: mixing multiple LoRAs with learned routing is closely related to mixture-of-LoRA-expert work [13,36,59,64] and to basis decomposition of LoRA weight spaces [12]; the contribution is a sensible adaptation of these ideas to the analogy task rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Societal impact and failure modes beyond one sentence ('may still struggle with tasks significantly different from the training corpus') are not discussed; examples of failure cases would be valuable given the editing application.
Minor presentation issues: several typos ('Aadpter', 'appraoch', 'Analogy results' figure captions), and Table 1's '+' row notation is ambiguous about which variants are cumulative.

strengths: The core idea—jointly training a basis of LoRA adapters with a lightweight router that composes them per input analogy—is well-motivated, clearly positioned relative to prior work (Dravid et al.'s weight-space interpolation, LoraHub, MoE-LoRA, hypernetwork approaches), and avoids the costly test-time optimization required by per-sample methods like DIA and PairEdit.

The paper includes a fairly comprehensive empirical study: comparisons against four recent analogy baselines plus adapted DIA and PairEdit variants in the appendix, an ablation over basis size, rank, activation function, encoder input layout, and encoder choice, an efficiency analysis showing only ~3% runtime overhead, and a user study validating the VLM-based evaluation protocol (66.7% user-VLM agreement vs. 74.2% user-user agreement).

The experiments specifically probing whether the model relies on the analogy pair rather than only the text prompt (Figs. 7-8, reduced-detail prompt ablation) directly support the central claim that the method performs demonstration-based, not just text-based, editing.

Limitations and failure cases are honestly discussed (struggles with tasks far from the training corpus, multi-component transformations, small edits, and the difficulty of obtaining aligned reference pairs in the wild), which strengthens the scientific case.

The method retains a clean theoretical property—a single rank-r' LoRA is a special case of LoRWeB when the router collapses—which helps interpret why the approach is more expressive than single-adapter fine-tuning.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies on a custom, relatively small benchmark (540 self-constructed triplets across 90 tasks plus the 10-task Relation252k unseen set). The construction involves LLM-generated prompts, community LoRAs, and filtering steps (e.g., filtering prompts where Flux.1-Kontext fails to produce a meaningful edit), which introduces potential selection bias that is not fully analyzed; a standard public benchmark comparison would strengthen the case.

Quantitative results depend heavily on Gemma-3 as judge. Although the appendix validates user-VLM agreement (66.7%) against user-user agreement (74.2%), 66.7% is meaningfully below inter-human agreement, and win rates in Fig. 6 over the strongest baseline (LoRA r=128: 57.6% user / 57.9% VLM) are modest; statistical significance is not reported.

Novelty is incremental: routing over a mixture of learned LoRAs is closely related to existing mixture-of-LoRA-expert work [13, 43, 70], and the conceptual inspiration (LoRA weight bases spanning semantic spaces) is explicitly borrowed from [12]. The contribution is the application and joint-training scheme to visual analogies, which is reasonable but not a fundamentally new technique.

Several presentation issues suggest insufficient polish: broken LaTeX in Eqs. (1), (2), (4) and (5) rendering labels as raw text, typos ('inot', 'aplpied', 'Analogyist', 'Aadpter', 'peron's', 'lead' vs. 'led', 'Join training'), inconsistent citations (EditTransfer vs. Edit-Transfer), and a malformed URL footnote (https://https://huggingface.co/). These do not undermine the science but reduce clarity and professionalism.

The comparison to VisualCloze and EditTransfer uses models built on Flux.1-Dev while the proposed method uses Flux.1-Kontext, a newer editing-specialized backbone; the parameter-matched Flux.1-Kontext LoRA baseline partially controls for this, but backbone confounds in cross-model comparisons are not fully disentangled.

Training uses only 10K steps on a single H100 with limited implementation detail on router initialization and training dynamics (e.g., whether the router collapses to constant weights early); reproducibility would benefit from more detail, and the promised code release is only referenced via a 'website' placeholder.

strengths: The paper is clearly written, with a well-motivated problem (visual analogy editing), a coherent method description, and thorough related-work coverage positioning LoRWeB against LoraHub, Mixture-of-LoRA experts, and the weight-basis observations of Dravid et al.

The evaluation is relatively comprehensive: comparisons against four recent baselines (RelationAdapter, VisualCloze, EditTransfer, matched-capacity single LoRA) plus per-sample optimization methods (DIA, PairEdit) in the appendix, a user study, ablations over basis size, rank, activation, encoder input layout, and encoder backbone, and a documented user-VLM agreement analysis.
The method is efficient and practical: the router adds only ~3% inference overhead and requires no test-time optimization, which is a genuine advantage over DIA/PairEdit.

The analysis of whether the model actually uses the analogy pair rather than the text prompt (Figs. 7, 8, App. B.5) is a thoughtful experiment that goes beyond generic editing evaluations, and failure cases are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: jointly training a set of LoRA adapters with a learned, input-conditioned routing mechanism is a well-established pattern (mixture-of-LoRA experts, LoraHub-style composition); the contribution is essentially an application of this known recipe to the visual analogy task rather than a new mechanism or new insight into LoRA weight spaces, despite the 'spanning the analogy space' framing.

The core claim — that a dynamic basis beats a single matched-capacity LoRA — is only weakly supported: the pairwise win rate against the capacity-matched r=128 LoRA is 57.9% (VLM) and 57.6% (user study), barely above chance, while the headline 'state-of-the-art' impression comes mostly from comparisons against methods with different design goals. This marginal margin does not clearly justify the added architectural complexity.

Heavy reliance on Gemma-3 as the primary quantitative judge (Preservation, Edit Accuracy, Pairwise VLM) is fragile; the 66.7% human-VLM agreement (vs. 74.2% user-user) reported in App. A.4 actually indicates the VLM is a noisier judge than humans, and no results on a standard, externally validated benchmark for this task are provided.

The evaluation set is small and partly self-constructed: 540 custom triplets with Flux-generated reference pairs (mitigated but not eliminated by App. B.6), and a user study of only 33 users over 45 image pairs — too few pairs for confident statistical conclusions, and filtering out cases where no method succeeded may bias the comparison.

The motivating hypothesis about a meaningful 'space of LoRAs' is never validated: no analysis of the learned basis vectors (do different LoRAs specialize in interpretable transformation types? do interpolations behave semantically?), which leaves the conceptual contribution of the paper unsubstantiated by evidence.

Some methodological choices feel under-explored and the results are somewhat inconsistent: e.g., why softmax beats Tanh is only speculated, larger bases (N=64) hurt performance without a clear explanation, and the advantage of separating image encoding from the 2x2 grid is modest in the ablation table.

strengths: The core idea is well motivated and clearly presented: instead of a single LoRA that must capture the whole space of visual transformations, LoRWeB learns a jointly-trained basis of LoRA adapters plus a lightweight routing encoder, allowing task-specific adapter composition in a single forward pass. This is a sensible and novel transfer of weight-basis insights (e.g., Dravid et al., LoraHub) from concept personalization/NLP to visual analogy editing.

The method is efficient and practical: inference overhead is minimal (~3% runtime increase over a single LoRA), with no test-time optimization, contrasting favorably with per-sample-optimization methods (DIA, PairEdit) that need tens of minutes per image.

The experimental protocol is unusually thorough for this area: comparisons to four strong baselines plus adapted variants of DIA (DIA-Kontext) and PairEdit, a user study (33 users), a validation of VLM-vs-human agreement (66.7% agreement vs. 74.2% inter-user agreement), ablations over basis size, rank, activation function, encoder input layout, and encoder backbone (SigLIP2), plus failure-case analysis and robustness checks (non-identical reference pairs, non-Flux-generated references, prompt/analogy misalignment).

The analysis of analogy-vs-prompt dependence (Figs. 7-8, reduced-detail prompt ablation) directly substantiates the claim that the model genuinely leverages the analogy pair rather than the text prompt, addressing a plausible confounder in this task family.

The paper is honest about limitations (struggles with out-of-corpus transformations, multi-component edits, small detail edits), and positions the contribution appropriately as an architecture/composition contribution rather than claiming maximal capacity is the answer.
weaknesses: The evaluation set is largely self-constructed: 540 of 840 triplets are built by the authors using LLM-generated prompts and Flux.1-Kontext (and community LoRAs) to generate reference pairs. This creates a potential circularity risk in the generalization claims, and the filtering step (dropping prompts where Flux fails a meaningful edit) narrows the task distribution in ways that are hard to audit. Only 10 unseen tasks from Relation252k are publicly available.

Margins over the most important control - a single LoRA of matched capacity (r=128) - are modest: user preference 57.6% vs. 42.4%, pairwise VLM 57.9%, and LoRWeB actually has slightly worse LPIPS (0.31 vs 0.27) and only marginally better CLIP directional similarity (0.21 vs 0.20). The headline improvement over per-sample-optimization baselines is less meaningful given those methods' much weaker backbones or extreme compute cost. The generality claim would benefit from stronger separation on the held-out Relation252k unseen split specifically.

Heavy reliance on VLM (Gemma-3) scoring for primary quantitative results. Although the authors report reasonable human-VLM agreement, VLM-based pairwise preferences on generative imagery are known to have biases (e.g., toward stylistic consistency), and the ablation table's fine-grained distinctions (e.g., 57.9 vs 60.4 vs 59.9) are likely within noise, yet are used to draw conclusions about basis size importance.

The ablation presentation is confusing: in Table 1, rows labeled with '+' (e.g., '+ r = 16', '+ Tanh activation') read as additions but are actually ablations/replacements, and the '+' convention obscures which configuration corresponds to which result. Some LPIPS/CLIP-directional ablation numbers move counter to the pairwise VLM preferences without discussion.

The analogy task still assumes an aligned reference pair {a, a'} that isolates the transformation; the paper acknowledges this and shows partial robustness, but this remains a substantial practical limitation for 'in the wild' use, and the promising direction of disentangling transformation components is left to future work.

Presentation has numerous typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'Aadpter', 'Edit Transfer' vs 'EditTransfer', 'backpropegating', 'inot', 'evluations', mixed naming of Fig. 4 column headers, malformed LaTeX artifacts in the source of Eqs. 1-4), and the special-case rank argument in Sec. 3.2 is informal rather than precise.
